title: Woodland Park Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Woodland Park wells have a 200 ft median depth, 6.2 gpm median yield, and finished well costs of about $19,000-$32,000.
h1: Wells and Water in Woodland Park, Colorado
intro_html:
Buying land near Woodland Park means dealing primarily with mountain bedrock, not the shallow basin conditions found in some other parts of Colorado. The permitted-well records within 5 miles show a median well depth of 200 feet and a median reported pump yield of 6.2 gallons per minute.

Most permits are for domestic or household use, and nearly all named aquifers are unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers. That makes neighboring well records useful, but it does not make a specific lot predictable. A driller still needs to evaluate access, geology, casing, grout, pumping equipment, and the intended household use.

sections.heading: Woodland Park well depth follows the mountain bedrock
sections.html:
The median reported depth is 200 feet. The middle half of wells runs from 120 to 380 feet, so a bid based only on the median can be too low or too high for a particular lot. The 90th-percentile depth is 500 feet, and the deepest record reaches 3,535 feet.

Depths are spread across the area: 18% are under 100 feet, 44% are between 100 and 300 feet, 33% are between 300 and 600 feet, and 5% are deeper than 600 feet. Most permits identify fractured bedrock, commonly granite or gneiss in this mountain setting. Fractures control where water is found, which is why nearby depths help with planning but cannot guarantee the result.

sections.heading: A Woodland Park well usually makes usable household water
sections.html:
Among wells with reported pump yields, the median is 6.2 gallons per minute and the middle half is 2.0 to 9.8 gallons per minute. That range is generally relevant to a household, but the pump, pressure tank, storage, and well recovery rate still matter. A yield test should be reviewed rather than relying on the permit number alone.

Six percent of reported yields are under 1 gallon per minute. Another 34% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, while 52% are between 5 and 15 gallons per minute and 8% exceed 15 gallons per minute. Colorado exempt household-use wells have a 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit. Confirm the permit's actual use and limits before planning irrigation, livestock, or other demands.

sections.heading: Water levels near Woodland Park need a current check
sections.html:
Reported static water levels have a median depth of 85 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 60 to 115 feet. That measurement is not the same as the depth of the well or the pumping level while water is being used. It is a snapshot taken when the well was measured.

The decade comparison does not show a simple dropping trend in these records. The median static level was 108 feet below surface in the 2010s and 98 feet in the 2020s, meaning the later reported median was shallower. Only 71 wells report a static water level, so treat this as limited local evidence rather than a guarantee for an unbuilt lot. Ask for a current well test and water-level measurement when buying an existing property.

sections.heading: Permit history shows long use and current drilling activity
sections.html:
The records include 2,407 permitted wells, with 1,546 recorded as constructed. Total depth is reported for 1,596 wells, pump yield for 805, and static water level for 71. Permits were issued across the area from the 1950s through the 2020s, with the newest permit year listed as 2025.

The busiest decades were the 1970s with 377 permits, the 1980s with 403, and the 1990s with 477. The leading names in the records are Woods Drilling Inc. under Woods, William D., with 358 permits; Mountain Well Improvement LLC under Wiley, David D., with 288; and Woods Drilling Inc. under Woods, William L., with 269. A permit record is not a performance guarantee, so verify current licensing, references, insurance, and the proposed contract.

sections.heading: What a new Woodland Park well can cost
sections.html:
In fractured mountain bedrock, the drilling rate used for this area is about $65 to $100 per foot. At the 200-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $13,000 to $20,000. That is drilling only, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $19,000 to $32,000 at the median depth. A 380-foot well, a difficult access route, extra casing or grout, greater power distance, or a failed first hole can change the final bill. Get the driller to state what is included, the assumed depth, the treatment of additional footage, and which site-work items remain separate.

sections.heading: Checks that matter before building near Woodland Park
sections.html:
Low yield and dry holes are the main geological concerns in fractured granite and gneiss. The records show 6% of reported yields under 1 gallon per minute, so ask how the contractor handles a low-producing well, storage, deepening, or a replacement hole. Do not treat a high nearby yield as proof that your parcel will perform the same way.

Environmental screening also deserves attention. Within about 10 miles are 7 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 16 historic mine features, and 9 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These mapped locations do not automatically mean a property is contaminated. Test the well water through a qualified laboratory and review nearby land uses. Confirm septic setbacks, soil suitability, driveway access, utility trenching, and the building envelope before drilling.

sections.heading: A practical lot decision for Cascade-Chipita Park and nearby areas
sections.html:
Start by collecting permits and well-test records for the target parcel and nearby properties, including Cascade-Chipita Park and Green Mountain Falls, each listed about 5 miles away. Divide is about 7 miles away, while the Air Force Academy is about 10 miles away. These comparisons can help a driller plan, but fractured-bedrock conditions can change quickly across short distances.

Before closing, make the well permit, measured yield, static level, laboratory water test, septic approval, and access plan part of the review. If the lot is vacant, obtain a written drilling proposal and ask what happens if the hole is deeper than expected or produces less than planned. If the basin or permit requires it, confirm any augmentation-plan requirement before assuming the well can support the intended use.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Woodland Park?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Woodland Park is 200 feet. The middle half runs from 120 to 380 feet, while the 90th percentile is 500 feet. About 18% are under 100 feet, 44% are 100 to 300 feet, and 33% are 300 to 600 feet. Fractured mountain bedrock makes individual depths variable.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Woodland Park?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses about $65 to $100 per foot. At the 200-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $13,000 to $20,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is about $19,000 to $32,000. Access, extra depth, casing, grout, and difficult geology can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water does a Woodland Park well produce?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 6.2 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 2.0 to 9.8 gallons per minute. Six percent of reported yields are under 1 gallon per minute. Because only 805 wells report a pump yield, request the actual well test and recovery information for the property rather than relying only on area averages.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Woodland Park?
faq.a: The area includes 7 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 16 historic mine features, and 9 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those locations do not establish contamination at a particular home. Have the well tested by a qualified laboratory, review nearby environmental records, and retest after ownership or land-use changes.

faq.q: Are Woodland Park wells running out of water?
faq.a: The available static-level records do not show a simple decline: the median was 108 feet below surface in the 2010s and 98 feet in the 2020s. However, only 71 wells report static water levels. That is limited evidence, not a guarantee. For a property purchase, review the current static level, pumping test, recovery, and seasonal conditions.
